extracted.intended_audience: Undergraduates and first- or second-year graduate students applying to the NSF GRFP (NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, applicant-facing guidance for preparing NSF GRFP submissions: required essays, how to address the two review criteria (Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts), structural suggestions for each essay, and related procedural tips (letters, field choice, audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are instructed to evaluate the potential for the proposed activity to advance knowledge and understanding within its own field or across different fields. Consider whether the activities suggest and explore creative, original, or potentially transformative concepts; whether the plan is well-reasoned, well-organized, and based on a sound rationale; whether the plan incorporates a mechanism to assess success; how well qualified the individual is to conduct the proposed activities; and whether adequate resources are available to the PI (at the home organization or through collaborations) to carry out the proposed activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: the potential to benefit society and contribute to the achievement of specific, desired societal outcomes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader impacts may be accomplished through the research itself, through activities that are directly related to specific research projects, or through activities that are supported by, but are complementary to, the project. Examples of societally relevant outcomes include (but are not limited to): full participation of underrepresented groups in STEM; improved STEM education and educator development; increased public scientific literacy and public engagement; improved well-being of individuals in society; development of a diverse STEM workforce; increased partnerships between academia and industry; improved national security; increased U.S. economic competitiveness; and enhanced infrastructure for research and education. Address how your experiences and plans indicate potential for future broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants must include separate statements on IM and BI
rubrics_metrics.description: applicants must include separate statements on Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts in their written statements in order to provide reviewers with the information necessary to evaluate the application with respect to both Criteria
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly include separate discussions of Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts in each essay as required by NSF. The page repeatedly emphasizes having explicit headers labeled 'Intellectual Merit' and 'Broader Impacts' so reviewers can find and evaluate these sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Statement, Relevant Background, and Future Goals (essay prompt & length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Please outline your educational and professional development plans and career goals; how graduate school will prepare you to contribute to expanding scientific understanding and broadly benefit society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format: 3 pages. Suggested internal structure: Personal Statement (~1 page) to tell your unique story and highlight broader impacts; Relevant Background (~1 page) to explain research experience and prepare for graduate school (mainly Intellectual Merit); Future Goals (~1/2 page) to tie personal and scientific background into a cohesive vision. Conclude with short (~1/4 page each) explicit headers for 'Intellectual Merit' and 'Broader Impacts' summarizing contributions. Use specific examples of research and roles, indicate independent vs team contributions, and highlight results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate Research Statement (essay prompt & length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an original research topic to pursue in graduate school; describe the research idea, general approach, resources needed, literature context, and address potential to advance knowledge and broader impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format: 2 pages. Recommended structure: Introduction (introduce scientific problem and its impact on science and society); Research Plan (major steps, creative aspects, alternatives for hard steps, your skills to execute); explicit 'Intellectual Merit' header to show impact and how you hit review criteria; explicit 'Broader Impacts' header; optional Conclusion summarizing project. Emphasize the creative part, alternatives, measures of success, and resources/collaborations required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Criterion — GRFP: Intellectual Merit (holistic applicant evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: the potential of the applicant to advance knowledge based on a holistic analysis of the complete application, including the Personal, Relevant Background, and Future Goals Statement, Graduate Research Plan Statement, strength of the academic record, description of previous research experience or publication/presentations, and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For GRFP reviewers, Intellectual Merit is assessed across the whole application; therefore applicants should ensure that personal statements, research plan, academic record, documented research experience, and reference letters all coherently demonstrate potential to advance knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Criterion — GRFP: Broader Impacts (holistic applicant evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: the potential of the applicant for future broader impacts as indicated by personal experiences, professional experiences, educational experiences and future plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader Impacts for GRFP are assessed holistically: include examples from your personal, educational, and professional experiences and clearly indicate future plans that would realize broader impacts. Use concrete evidence and past activities to justify projected impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review elements to be considered for both criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The following elements should be considered in the review for both criteria: potential to advance knowledge/benefit society; extent to which proposed activities suggest creative/original/transformative concepts; whether plan is well-reasoned/organized/based on sound rationale and includes mechanism to assess success; qualifications of individual/team; adequacy of resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly address each element where relevant in your essays: state how the work advances knowledge or benefits society, highlight creativity/transformative potential, provide a clear, reasoned plan with success metrics, show your qualifications, and document available resources or collaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a general science audience (assume reviewer in primary field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for a general science audience and assume the reviewer is in your primary field, but not your subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, non-specialist language for subfield details; avoid jargon or define it; emphasize the broader significance and understandable rationale since reviewers may not be experts in your exact niche. The page notes NSF's tentative review panels guarantee only that the reviewer is in your primary field.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF funds the person, not the project
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF GRFP funds the person, not the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the application on demonstrating your potential, qualifications, and trajectory as an emerging scientist and leader, not solely on proposing a fixed, long-term project. Show how the research plan demonstrates your capabilities rather than promising NSF you will necessarily pursue exactly that project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary field selection guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important choice you make is designating the primary field (Chemistry vs Physics & Astronomy, etc). The subfield is less important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are an undergrad doing research, make your proposal related to what you are currently researching provided (1) you will apply to programs in the same primary field and (2) there is at least a small chance you could do something related to your proposal in graduate school. NSF will not force you to follow through; they want to see you can write a proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of reference: number and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: You will need to get at least three letters of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask early and remind writers of the deadline. Get a diverse set of letter writers who collectively address Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts (author's example: one current adviser doing similar research, a past research adviser, and a work supervisor so two letters address intellectual merit and one addresses broader impacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-focused checklist (author's 'two cents')
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical checklist of points to be able to answer for BOTH Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts: How would answering this research question change science (IM) or society (BI)? Why should I fund you specifically, and not just this research question? What innovation do you specifically bring to the table? Is there a detailed plan with built-in measures of success? What are your qualifications? Can you actually carry out the needed research?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of each essay, be able to check off how you answered each of these points for both criteria. Use the checklist to structure and conclude essays so reviewers can readily find answers to these evaluative questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and organization expectations (headers, structure, page limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays have specific page limits and should include explicit headers for Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal, Relevant Background, and Future Goals = 3 pages total; Graduate Research Statement = 2 pages. Use clear headers (e.g., 'Intellectual Merit', 'Broader Impacts') and the recommended section breakdowns (Personal, Relevant Background, Future Goals; Introduction, Research Plan, IM, BI, Conclusion) to make reviewer assessment easier. The page also references official NSF formatting and suggests consulting NSF guidance and FAQs.
